items.title: Martin Heinrich faces backlash from tribes over permitting deal
items.author: Josh Siegel
items.quote: Opposition from Native American tribes is emerging as a threat to the Senate's bipartisan permitting reform bill, a particular problem for Democrats who often support tribal priorities.
items.speaker: Josh Siegel
facts: NATHPO calls the bill a 'legislative assault on the sovereignty of Tribal nations' and, with several other large tribal groups, sent a letter to Senate leaders urging 'the immediate rescission of this language'.
Democratic source close to negotiations: 'Renegotiating what is a carefully balanced product would imperil Democratic wins on transmission and other policies.'

Ira Matt, NATHPO executive director: 'For Sen. Heinrich, it's a very short-sighted approach. This isn't going to bode well back in his home state because tribes see through this. They know it's a farce.'
Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) suggested she could oppose the bill; protecting 'tribal sovereignty, the rights of our communities, and the environment will always be my line in the sand.'

Ben Schifman, Institute for Progress: 'This was a pretty even compromise, changing around the edges some excesses of the 106 process, but writing into the law for the first time stuff that's important to tribes.'
Heinrich's office did not respond to a request for comment. New Mexico has 23 federally recognized tribes.

items.title: Pressure on Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries to reject permitting reform
items.quote: Dozens of progressive environmental groups sent a letter today to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, which we exclusively obtained, urging Democrats to oppose the bipartisan permitting reform bill to speed up federal approvals of energy projects.
items.speaker: Punchbowl News
facts: Preview only (premium). Confirms the 222-group letter date (Oct 5) and recipients.

items.title: Rush to cut permitting red tape runs into law to protect America's historic sites
items.author: Lindsey McPherson
items.speaker: Greg Werkheiser
items.quote: This legislation will effectively end the 60-year-old process of historic preservation in America.
facts: Greg Werkheiser is founding partner of Cultural Heritage Partners (a law firm, sector: other/academic not environmental_group).
Terry Klein, chair of the Society for Historical Archaeology: in the context of historic preservation the bill 'does exactly the opposite' of expediting projects.
Opponents say the bill narrows projects subject to Section 106 review, removes the public as a consulted party and infringes on tribal and state rights.
